page.h1: HTS Chapter 40: Rubber and Articles Thereof — Export Markets & Foreign Tariffs on U.S. Goods

seo.title: What Canada, Mexico, China & the EU Charge on U.S. Tires & Rubber (HTS Ch. 40) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Tariffs on U.S. tires, gaskets, hoses and synthetic rubber in Canada, Mexico, the EU, Brazil, Australia, China, Chile, India and Japan, with each market's tire rules.

intro: Six of the nine largest markets charge nothing on qualifying U.S. tires: Canada and Mexico under USMCA, Chile and Australia under their FTAs, Japan (0% MFN on tires and synthetic rubber) and, since July 1, 2026, the EU. **Mexico** is the one to watch on paperwork: tires that fail the USMCA rule of origin pay 25–35% since January 2026. **China** adds 10% to its 7.5–25% rates on every U.S. good, its older counter-tariffs apply unless the buyer holds an exclusion, and three U.S. synthetic rubbers pay anti-dumping duties of 75.5% to 222%. **Brazil** has no trade agreement with the U.S. and charges its Mercosur rates (12% on EPDM, 16% on gaskets); it has approved 30% on all imported car tires for 12 months. What usually decides access for tires is the buyer's safety certification (Canada's and Mexico's tire standards, the EU's E-mark, China's CCC, India's BIS mark, Brazil's INMETRO seal), covered under each market's regulator below.
valueBasis: FOB value of U.S. exports, as reported by the United States to UN Comtrade.

assumptions: Each cell shows the rate for one representative six-digit subheading per heading: the line with the largest 2025 U.S. exports (for example 4011.80 for new tires, 4016.93 for gaskets and seals, 4002.70 for synthetic rubber). Car-tire (4011.10) and truck-tire (4011.20) rates are named in the basis where they differ. National 8–10-digit lines can differ.

MFN rates are World Bank/UNCTAD WITS (TRAINS) applied rates (2023, Chile 2022), checked against the market's own 2026 schedule where available: EU TARIC, the Customs Tariff Schedules of Japan (April 1, 2026) and the Australian Border Force working tariff (July 1, 2026).

USMCA (Canada, Mexico), the U.S.–Chile FTA and the U.S.–Australia FTA apply 0% to qualifying U.S.-origin goods; the normal-rate column shows the MFN rate for goods that do not qualify. Mexico's column includes the general rates raised from January 1, 2026.
For the EU, Regulation (EU) 2026/1455 takes Chapter 40 to 0% for U.S. goods from July 1, 2026; the normal-rate column shows the EU rate before then.

China's cells add the 10% extra duty on all U.S. goods to the MFN rate. China's 2018–2019 counter-tariffs (Tariff Commission Announcement 2018 No. 7 List 2, Announcement 2019 No. 3 and the September 2019 list of Announcement 2019 No. 4, halved by Announcement 2020 No. 1) are named in each basis but not added, because importers can hold exclusions valid until December 31, 2026. Anti-dumping duties on U.S. EPDM, halobutyl and chloroprene rubber are shown on heading 4002 only.

Brazil's cells use WITS 2023 Mercosur rates. Brazil moves some lines above or below the common tariff through its exception lists, as with car tires (4011.10) and steel-cord conveyor belts (4010.11) in November 2026, so the 2026 applied rate can differ.
India's rates are the basic customs duty (WITS 2023) only; surcharges and IGST are not included, and the U.S.–India framework has not been implemented as far as we found.
Canada's 25% surtax on U.S. tires (March 4 to August 31, 2025) is not in the rates because it has been repealed; no Chapter 40 item is on Canada's September 2026 surtax list.
